How big was the
monster of the Devonian seas?
For decades, popular books
said Dunkleosteus reached
nine meters.
A 2023 study says
the largest were only
about three and a half.
Why did the legend
grow so large,
and what else did
we get wrong about
Paleozoic giants?
Dunkleosteus was a
placoderm, one of the
armored fish, with a
heavily armored head.
It had no true teeth.
Instead, its jaws carried
sharp bony plates that
sharpened against each
other as they worked.
A 2023 study reexamined
its skull and body
proportions.
It concluded that the
largest Dunkleosteus were
only about three and
a half meters long,
shorter and stockier than
once believed, but still
about as heavy as
a great white shark
more than four meters long.
The real animal was
smaller than the legend,
but no less dangerous.
Now go back to the Cambrian.
Anomalocaris, whose name
means unusual shrimp,
was one of the
first large predators.
Older books said it
reached a meter long.
Newer studies suggest the
largest were closer to
forty centimeters, still
a giant in a
world where most animals
were a few centimeters long.
But here is a twist.
Its round mouth was
small, and the plates
around it show very
little wear.
Many researchers now think
Anomalocaris could not
crack hard shells,
and instead hunted
soft-bodied prey, perhaps
sucking it in.
The picture of a
monster crunching through
armored animals may be
more legend than fact.
The Ordovician seas had
giants too.
The largest animals were
nautiloids, relatives of
today's squid and nautilus.
Cameroceras, with a long,
straight, cone-shaped shell,
is often said to
have reached nine meters,
but that number rests
on a doubtful old report.
Well-supported specimens
point to shells of
around two meters.
Put them side by side.
Anomalocaris was once said
to reach a meter,
but the best estimate
is now under forty
centimeters.
Cameroceras was said to
reach nine meters,
but well-supported shells
suggest about two.
And Dunkleosteus, once
nine meters, is now
estimated at about three
and a half.
Bigger stories travel faster
than careful measurements.
The giants of the
Paleozoic were real,
just not always as
large as the legends.
The full journey,
from the Cambrian Explosion
to the Great Dying,
is on Miya's Lab.
